\section{Overview}

INPUT--MODULE16 reads up to 16 switches via direct connection (2 headers~\texttimes~8 inputs each) and generates MIDI NOTE ON/OFF or PROGRAM CHANGE messages. No diode matrix or encoding is required.

It supports both traditional 5-pin DIN MIDI and USB-MIDI output with automatic merging of incoming MIDI data. In addition to standard MIDI capabilities, the module introduces several advanced features such as a High-Speed Analog MIDI Bus and an easy-to-use Wi-Fi configuration interface accessible via a web browser.

\section{Features}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Board dimensions 141\texttimes{}34~mm
    \item Powered via 5~V DC / 0.1~A
    \item Reads up to 16 switches via direct connection
    \item MIDI IN (5-pin DIN)
    \item MIDI OUT (5-pin DIN) with automatic merging of MIDI IN and internal messages
    \item USB MIDI output (class-compliant)
    \item Optional High-Speed Analog MIDI Bus -- supports up to 4\texttimes{} the standard MIDI baud rate for expanded bandwidth
    \item Wi-Fi Configuration Interface -- configure module settings via a web browser by connecting to the module's built-in Wi-Fi access point
\end{itemize}

\section{Introduction to MIDI Device Connectivity and Latency Considerations}

In practical applications, it is common to use multiple MIDI modules in a setup, often combining devices from various manufacturers. There are two basic approaches to connecting input MIDI devices to an end device such as a computer or Digital Audio Workstation (DAW).


\begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.2\textwidth]{Analog_chaining.drawio.png}
    \caption{Chaining via the analog MIDI bus -- this typically involves using traditional 5-pin DIN connectors (though other connectors may also be used).}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth]{USB_star.drawio.png}
    \caption{Connecting in a "star" topology via USB.}
\end{figure}

\begin{center}
    \fbox{
    \begin{minipage}{0.95\linewidth}
        \faInfoCircle~\textbf{Note: Latency considerations} If you prefer chaining via the analog MIDI bus and use many MIDI devices, latency can become a significant issue. The transmission of a single standard MIDI message takes approximately 1\,ms. As MIDI data is passed through multiple devices in the chain, this latency can accumulate and become noticeable.
    \end{minipage}
    }
\end{center}

One of the key features of the INPUT--MODULE16 is its optional High-Speed Analog MIDI Bus mode. When activated, MIDI messages are transmitted at four times the standard MIDI speed. However, please note that this high-speed mode is not compatible with third-party MIDI devices, as they are designed to operate at the standard MIDI baud rate.

\subsection{Power}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Voltage: 5~V DC (regulated)
  \item Current Consumption: 0.1~A max
\end{itemize}

The module can be powered directly via USB. A dedicated external power supply is only required when powering multiple modules together

\begin{center}
    \fbox{
    \begin{minipage}{0.95\linewidth}
        \faInfoCircle~\textbf{Note:}
        \begin{itemize}
            \item Use a regulated 5~V supply. Do not exceed 5.3~V. Reverse polarity can damage the device.
            \item When powering many modules together, use a dedicated power supply with sufficient current capacity or a suitable powered USB hub.
        \end{itemize}
    \end{minipage}
    }
\end{center}

\subsection{Switch Inputs}

The board provides two 16-pin IDC headers (Inputs~1 and Inputs~2), each with 8 input pins and 8 paired GND pins. Each pair (signal + GND) is adjacent on the header, so you can simply take one pair from a flat ribbon cable, solder one wire to the switch terminal and the other to the switch's ground connection --- no need to create a shared common ground wire. The board handles the pull-up internally, so no external resistors are required.

\begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=1\textwidth]{switches-wiring.png}
    \caption{Direct switch wiring diagram}
\end{figure}

\begin{center}
    \fbox{
    \begin{minipage}{0.95\linewidth}
        \faInfoCircle~\textbf{Note:}
        \begin{itemize}
            \item Each header provides 8 input pins, each with its own dedicated GND neighbour.
            \item The board handles the pull-up internally -- no external resistors needed.
            \item The module is not designed for diode matrix scanning or velocity sensing.
        \end{itemize}
    \end{minipage}
    }
\end{center}

\section{Setting Up the Module - Wi-Fi Access Point Mode}

You can conveniently set up the module using any web browser on your computer or mobile phone. The module can start in a special mode where it creates a Wi-Fi access point that you can connect to.

\begin{enumerate}
    \item Unplug the module from any power source (USB and external power).
    \item Press and hold the WiFi button.
    \item Continue holding the button while powering on the module (e.g., by connecting an external power source).
    \item The Status LED will light up steadily, indicating that the module is now in Wi-Fi access
    point mode.
    \item On your computer (with a Wi-Fi adapter) or smartphone, go to the Wi-Fi settings. You
    should see a new Wi-Fi network named "Input Module16". Connect to it.

    \faInfoCircle~\textbf{Note}: While connected to this network, your device will lose access to the internet.
    \item Open a web browser (such as Google Chrome) and enter the following IP address in the address bar: 192.168.4.1 -- the fixed IP address of the MIDI module's web server. You should now see the settings page, as shown in the image below.
    \item Use the dropdown menus to configure all the necessary settings, then press the
    "Save Settings" button. If needed, you can restore the factory default values by
    pressing the "Reset to Defaults" button.
    \item Once you're done, disconnect the module from the power source. Your settings will be saved and automatically applied the next time the module starts.

    \faInfoCircle~\textbf{Note}: While in Wi-Fi access point mode, the module does not transmit MIDI data. MIDI communication is disabled during setup.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth]{app-settings-window.png}
    \caption{Settings page in Wi-Fi Access Point mode}
\end{figure}

The firmware provides a minimal HTTP-based settings page when the unit runs in Wi-Fi Access Point mode. The page allows configuring the following properties:

\begin{description}
  \item[MIDI serial bus rate] Toggle between the standard MIDI baud rate (31250) and a higher UART rate (115200). High-speed mode is not compatible with third-party MIDI equipment.
  \item[Input header 1 / Input header 2] Each header covers 8 inputs. The following settings are available per header:
    \begin{itemize}
      \item \textbf{MIDI channel} (range: 1--16)
      \item \textbf{Base MIDI number} (range: 0--119). The first input maps to this note; subsequent inputs increment the note number.
      \item \textbf{Message type}: NOTE ON/OFF or PROGRAM CHANGE.
      \item \textbf{Invert inputs}: NOTE ON/PROGRAM CHANGE when an input is activated or deactivated.
    \end{itemize}
\end{description}


\section{Status LED behavior}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Startup: brief blink sequence
  \item MIDI activity: short blink when MIDI bytes are transmitted
  \item AP mode: LED remains steadily lit while the AP is active
\end{itemize}
